justice: Road space is clearly allocated with multiple motor-vehicle lanes, marked turning arrows, and a physically separated median fence, indicating a structured distribution of movement space for different users.
Both sides show paved sidewalks with curbs and landscaped buffers, suggesting some provision of pedestrian space rather than vehicle-only design.

Barrier-free features (e.g., curb ramps, tactile paving, pedestrian push buttons) are not visible at this intersection approach, limiting confidence that access is equally usable for all abilities despite the presence of sidewalks.
safety: High-visibility zebra crosswalks and lane-direction arrows provide clear guidance and reduce ambiguity at the intersection.
A continuous metal median fence discourages unsafe mid-block crossing and channels crossing to designated crosswalk locations.

Very wide carriageway and multiple lanes imply higher vehicle speeds/exposure at crossings; no visible raised crosswalks, curb extensions, or protected intersection elements to shorten crossing distance.
livability: The corridor appears dominated by roadway and traffic control elements (multi-lane asphalt, large direction sign), with limited human-scale destinations or active frontage in view.
There are landscaped strips and grassed areas on the right, but they function more as buffers than as usable public space (no visible seating, plazas, or gathering nodes).
Low visible pedestrian activity and sparse street-level amenities (no shops, kiosks, or bus-stop facilities in frame) reduce perceived everyday convenience and street vitality.
sustainability: Street trees and planted buffers on both sides add some green infrastructure, supporting shade potential and basic ecological value over time.
The design appears to prioritize motor-vehicle throughput (wide lanes and multiple turn options), which tends to encourage driving over low-carbon modes.
No visible cycling facilities (bike lanes, cycle track separation, bicycle signals) or public transport elements (bus lane/stop) are evident, limiting sustainable mode support.
aesthetics: Clean, well-maintained pavement markings and orderly roadside planting create a tidy, legible visual environment.
Open views to distant hills/mountains provide positive scenic quality and a sense of spaciousness.
Large overhead signs, utility pylons, and extensive asphalt area make the streetscape feel infrastructure-heavy and less visually engaging at pedestrian eye level.
comfort: Tree canopy is sparse and young, offering limited shade; large exposed asphalt and open sky suggest potential heat and glare discomfort in warm/sunny conditions (thermal comfort).
Sidewalks appear smooth and unobstructed along the edges, supporting basic walking comfort, but there are no visible benches or resting features (physical comfort).
The wide road and likely higher speeds can reduce perceived comfort for non-motorized users when approaching the intersection due to noise and exposure (psychological comfort).
walkability: Marked crosswalks exist and appear aligned with the intersection geometry, supporting basic route continuity for pedestrians.
However, crossing distances are long due to the multi-lane width, and no median refuge island is clearly visible at the crosswalk to allow staged crossing.
Sidewalk environment lacks pedestrian amenities (seating, shade, active edges) and appears set along a high-capacity roadway, which reduces the attractiveness of walking.
bikeability: No bike lanes, shared-lane markings, or protected cycling infrastructure are visible on the approach, indicating low cycling provision.
The multi-lane intersection with several turning movements increases potential conflict points for cyclists, especially without dedicated signals or protected intersection design.
While pavement markings are clear for drivers, there are no visible cyclist-specific wayfinding elements (bike boxes, bicycle parking, or cycle crossing markings) to support comfortable cycling.
